title: A restless young man (1915)
hookLine: born in France, orphaned young, drifting through Cambridge and Columbia

lines: INTO THE CHURCHES FOR THE ART.
cards: Rome, 1933. An eighteen-year-old wanders the city on his own. Both his parents are dead.
He has money from a guardian, a head full of novels, and no plan. He goes into the old churches, not to pray, but to look at the mosaics, because he likes art.
Standing in front of those gold and blue walls, something catches in him that he can't name. He'll spend years running from it. His name is Thomas Merton.
He'll become the most well-known monk in America, and for the next eighteen days he's the guide. Today: a restless young man.

teach.b: First, the losses. Merton was born on January 31, 1915, in Prades, a small town in the south of France. His father was a painter from New Zealand, his mother an American artist.
When he was six, his mother died of cancer. When he was fifteen, his father died too.
Then he was moved around: schools in France and England, holidays with relatives, a guardian in London. A boy with a suitcase, never quite at home. Second, the drifting.
At Cambridge he drank, stayed out, failed at being careful, and left after a year he later looked back on with real shame. His guardian sent him to America.
At Columbia University in New York he was clever, funny, restless. He wrote for the humor magazine, loved jazz, and flirted with politics. Busy all the time, happy almost never.
Third, the mosaics. In those Roman churches he'd looked at pictures of Christ, and for the first time he wanted to know who that was. He didn't act on it yet.
He just couldn't forget it. Fourth, why restless is a start.

teach.h: RESTLESS UNTIL IT RESTS IN GOD.
teach.b: Long before Merton, Augustine wrote at the opening of his Confessions that the human heart is restless until it rests in God. Catholics have loved that sentence for sixteen hundred years.
It doesn't treat restlessness as a failure. It treats it as a sign you're made for something you haven't found yet.
Merton's early life looks like a mess. Read with Augustine, it looks like a search.

how: Many Catholics read Thomas Merton's autobiography as a modern story of conversion, and Augustine's line about the restless heart is often quoted in Catholic preaching and in the Catechism itself.

o: quiet, the stillness of a praying heart
restless, Augustine's word for the heart
unholy, a heart turned away from God

games.q: the young Merton — tap the pairs.

s: Merton grew up in a settled Catholic family
his parents were artists, both died when he was young, and he wasn't raised Catholic.
he first went into Rome's churches to look at the art
he went for the mosaics, and ended up wanting to know who the Christ in them was.
Augustine treats a restless heart as a sign of failure
he says the heart is restless until it rests in God: a sign you're made for more.

games.q: you're eighteen, alone in Rome, and something in a church mosaic moves you. what do you do?
o: notice it, then go on drifting for years
games.why: Merton didn't act on it for years. he went on drifting through Cambridge and Columbia, but he never forgot it.

practice: Get still, and notice what doesn't want to be still: the itch to check your phone, a thought that keeps circling, a sense that something's missing.

Don't fix it or scold it; find where it lives in your body, your chest, your hands, your jaw, and gently ask it what it's looking for, without needing an answer. If you pray, you can offer the restlessness itself.

wordCard.voice: Inquietum. Augustine's Latin word for restless, used here for Thomas Merton at eighteen: orphaned, gifted, drifting, and carrying one picture from Rome he couldn't shake. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: restless, the word Augustine uses for the heart in the opening of his Confessions.

carryVoice: Your line: restless is a start. The itch for something more can count as a beginning. Day two hundred seventy-two.
